```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, echo = FALSE)
library(here)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

res_dir <- here("analysis", "results")
fig_dir <- file.path(res_dir, "figures")
conv  <- readRDS(file.path(res_dir, "conventional_results.rds"))
bayes <- readRDS(file.path(res_dir, "bayesian_results.rds"))
sens  <- readRDS(file.path(res_dir, "bayesian_sensitivity.rds"))

annual <- conv$annual
st <- bayes$settings

# small helpers for writing numbers in the text
f1 <- function(x) sprintf("%.1f", x)
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)
ci <- function(lo, hi, f = f1) paste0("(", f(lo), ", ", f(hi), ")")

# one posterior summary row: model, quantity, region ("all", "early", "late")
ps <- function(model, quantity, region = "all") {
  tab <- if (region == "all") bayes$posterior_summary else bayes$posterior_by_region
  tab[tab$model == model & tab$quantity == quantity & tab$region == region, ]
}
# "mean (95% CrI)" for a posterior quantity
pci <- function(model, quantity, region = "all", f = f1) {
  r <- ps(model, quantity, region)
  paste0(f(r$mean), " ", ci(r$lower, r$upper, f))
}
pp <- function(i) bayes$post_probs$probability[i]
ppl <- sens$ppc_pvalues

w_b3 <- bayes$region_weights$B3
w_b4 <- bayes$region_weights$B4
loo_w <- bayes$loo_weights
conv_m1 <- conv$trend_rate |> filter(fit == "M1 AR1")
conv_m3 <- conv$estimates |> filter(fit == "M3 iid")
```

## 1. Scientific Question and Data

```{r data-overview}
n_years <- nrow(annual)
hottest <- annual |> arrange(desc(y)) |> slice_head(n = 3)
```

**Scientific question.** Has the average summer daily maximum temperature in
Austin, Texas, changed since 1938? If so, is the change better described as a
gradual trend or as an abrupt shift? If an abrupt shift is supported, when did
it most likely occur, how large was it, and how uncertain are its timing and
magnitude?

**Data.** We use daily maximum temperature (TMAX) from the NOAA Global
Historical Climatology Network–Daily [GHCN-D, @menne2012ghcnd] for the Austin
Camp Mabry station (GHCND:USW00013958), whose record begins in 1938. We kept
June 1 through August 31 observations, dropped values that were missing,
failed NOAA quality control or carried a measurement flag, and converted from
tenths of a degree to °C.

**Outcome.** For each year $t$, the outcome $Y_t$ is the mean daily maximum
temperature over that summer. A year is included only if at least 90% of its
92 summer days have a valid TMAX. Every summer from `r min(annual$year)` to
`r max(annual$year)` is complete, giving $n =$ `r n_years` annual
observations built from `r format(sum(annual$n_days), big.mark = ",")` daily
records.

**Predictors and features.** Calendar year is the only predictor; the
quantities of interest are the timing and size of any change. $Y_t$ ranges
from `r f1(min(annual$y))` °C to `r f1(max(annual$y))` °C (mean
`r f1(mean(annual$y))` °C, SD `r f1(sd(annual$y))` °C). Figure 1 shows large
year-to-year variability, and the three hottest summers
(`r paste(sort(hottest$year), collapse = ", ")`) all fall in the most recent
two decades, a pattern consistent with either a steady trend or a step change.
Because consecutive summers may be correlated, we also consider serially
correlated errors.

```{r fig-annual-series, fig.width=8, fig.height=3.5, fig.cap="**Figure 1.** Mean summer (June–August) daily maximum temperature at Austin Camp Mabry, 1938–2026. The grey line is a LOESS smoother shown for reference only."}
ggplot(annual, aes(year, y)) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(colour = "#2a78d6", size = 1.6) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Mean summer TMAX (°C)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

## 2. Bayesian Model

Let $s_t = t - 1982$ (year centred at the middle of the record). For all
models,
$$Y_t \mid \mu_t, \sigma \;\overset{\text{ind}}{\sim}\; \mathcal N(\mu_t, \sigma^2), \qquad t = 1938, \dots, 2026,$$
and the models differ only in the mean $\mu_t$:

| Model | Mean $\mu_t$ | Description |
|:--|:--|:--|
| B0 | $\alpha$ | no change |
| B1 | $\alpha + \beta s_t$ | linear trend |
| B2 | $\alpha + \beta s_t + \kappa s_t^2$ | quadratic trend |
| B3 | $\alpha + \beta s_t$ if $s_t < c$; $\;\alpha_2 + \beta (s_t - c)$ if $s_t \ge c$ | abrupt jump in level |
| B4 | $\alpha + \beta \min(s_t, c) + \beta_2 \{\max(s_t, c) - c\}$ | change in slope (joined) |
| B5 | $\alpha + \beta s_t$ if $s_t < c$; $\;\alpha_2 + \beta_2 (s_t - c)$ if $s_t \ge c$ | jump and slope change |

Here $\alpha$ is the mean summer TMAX in 1982 (on the first segment),
$\beta$ the warming rate (°C/year) and $\sigma$ the year-to-year standard
deviation. In the change-point models, $c$ is the change point, $\alpha_2$ is
the mean level immediately after the change, and $\beta_2$ the slope after
it. The jump size is the derived quantity
$\Delta = \alpha_2 - (\alpha + \beta c)$. We report the timing as
$\gamma = 1982 + \lceil c \rceil - 1$, the last summer before the change.

The six models answer the scientific question directly. B0 versus the others
asks *whether* temperature changed. B1 and B2 describe *gradual* change. B3–B5
describe an *abrupt* change whose timing $c$ is an unknown parameter with its
own posterior distribution [@carlin1992changepoint]. They are, one for one,
the Bayesian versions of the mean models M0–M5 of the conventional analysis
(Section 7), so the two analyses can be compared parameter by parameter.

We use independent normal errors. The conventional analysis found residual
autocorrelation only in the models with no change point (Section 7). We check
this assumption with AR(1) errors in Section 6.

## 3. Prior Distributions

```{r prior-table}
prior_tab <- tibble(
  Parameter = c("$\\alpha$, $\\alpha_2$ (level, °C)", "$\\beta$, $\\beta_2$ (slope, °C/year)",
                "$\\kappa$ (curvature)", "$\\sigma$ (°C)", "$c$ (change point)"),
  Prior = c(sprintf("$\\mathcal N(%g, %g^2)$", st$prior_mean[["int_1"]], st$prior_sd[["int_1"]]),
            sprintf("$\\mathcal N(0, %g^2)$", st$prior_sd[["s_1"]]),
            sprintf("$\\mathcal N(0, %g^2)$", st$prior_sd[["s_1_E2"]]),
            sprintf("Half-normal, scale %g", st$sigma_sd),
            sprintf("Uniform(%g, %g), i.e. 1952–2012", st$cp_lower, st$cp_upper)),
  Type = c("Weakly informative", "Weakly informative", "Weakly informative",
           "Weakly informative", "Non-informative within a window")
)
kable(prior_tab, caption = "**Table 1.** Prior distributions (same priors for every model in which a parameter appears).")
```

All priors are proper and **weakly informative**: they rule out physically
absurd values but are wide compared with what the data say.

* **Levels.** Central Texas summer afternoons average about 35 °C, so we
  centre $\alpha$ and $\alpha_2$ there. An SD of 3 °C gives 95% prior mass
  between about 29 and 41 °C. That range covers every summer mean seen in
  Texas and is about five times wider than the posterior turns out to be.
* **Slopes.** An SD of 0.05 °C/year places 95% prior mass within ±1 °C per
  decade. That is about five times the current global warming rate of
  roughly 0.2 °C per decade [@ipcc2018spm]. The prior is centred at zero, so
  it does not assume warming.
* **Curvature.** $\kappa \sim \mathcal N(0, 0.002^2)$ allows the quadratic
  term to bend the curve by up to about ±7 °C at the ends of the record.
* **Error SD.** A half-normal with scale 2 °C keeps $\sigma$ positive. Its
  median (1.3 °C) is close to the observed SD of $Y_t$, and it still allows
  values up to about 4 °C.
* **Change point.** A uniform prior on $c$ says every year is equally likely
  a priori. We restrict it to 1952–2012, the same 15% trimming used in the
  conventional sup-F test [@andrews1993tests]. A change in the first or last
  14 summers could not be told apart from a few unusual years.

A prior predictive check confirms these priors produce plausible data.
Simulating whole series from the B3 prior gives 95% of summer means between
`r f1(sens$prior_predictive$lower_2.5)` and
`r f1(sens$prior_predictive$upper_97.5)` °C. Only
`r pct(sens$prior_predictive$share_below_25 + sens$prior_predictive$share_above_45)`
fall outside 25–45 °C. The observed values
(`r f1(min(annual$y))`–`r f1(max(annual$y))` °C) sit well inside this range.
Figure 6 compares prior and posterior for the key quantities. Section 6 shows
that the estimated warming does not depend on these choices, but the
relative weight of the two change-point modes does.

## 4. Posterior Computation and Diagnostics

The models were written with the **mcp** package [@lindelov2020mcp], which
translates segment formulas into JAGS code [@plummer2003jags]. JAGS samples
the posterior with Gibbs sampling (slice sampling for parameters without
closed-form conditionals). Each model was run with
`r st$mcmc$chains` chains of `r format(st$mcmc$iter, big.mark = ",")` draws
after `r format(st$mcmc$adapt, big.mark = ",")` adaptation and burn-in
iterations. Every chain had its own fixed random seed.

**A multimodal posterior.** A first run of B3 started its chains at change
points spread over the prior range. The chains' average change years were
`r paste(round(bayes$naive_cp_by_chain), collapse = ", ")`. Each chain stays
for long stretches in either the 1960s or the 2000s, and $\widehat R$ for $c$ was
`r f2(bayes$naive_check$rhat[bayes$naive_check$variable == "cp_1"])`, far
above 1.01. The posterior of the change point has **two separate modes**, and
a Gibbs sampler cannot move between them. Taking the output of any single
chain would have been badly misleading.

**Remedy.** For a fixed $c$ and $\sigma$, every model is a normal linear
regression with normal priors, so the regression coefficients can be
integrated out exactly. That makes $p(c \mid y)$ computable on a fine grid
(integrating $\sigma$ numerically). We used the grid to compute the
posterior probability of each side of a split at 1987, between the two
modes. We then ran mcp separately with $c$ restricted to each side and
combined the two sets of draws in proportion to those probabilities. This is
exact, because
$p(\theta\mid y)=\sum_{r} P(r\mid y)\,p(\theta\mid y, r)$ over the two
regions $r$.

**Diagnostics.** Across all `r length(unique(bayes$convergence$run))` MCMC
runs, the largest rank-normalized $\widehat R$ [@vehtari2021rhat] is
`r sprintf("%.3f", max(bayes$convergence$rhat))`. The smallest bulk and tail
effective sample sizes are
`r format(round(min(bayes$convergence$ess_bulk)), big.mark = ",")` and
`r format(round(min(bayes$convergence$ess_tail)), big.mark = ",")`. Trace
plots (Figure 2) show well-mixed chains within each region.

As an independent check, the MCMC change-year probabilities match the exact
grid posterior almost perfectly (Figure 3); the region means agree to within
`r f1(max(abs(bayes$mcmc_vs_grid$mcmc_mean - bayes$mcmc_vs_grid$grid_mean)))`
years. We therefore trust the posterior summaries below.

```{r fig-trace, out.width="85%", fig.cap="**Figure 2.** Trace plots for the jump model B3, run separately with the change point restricted to before 1987 (top) and after 1987 (bottom). Colours are the four chains."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "bayes_trace.png"))
```

```{r fig-grid, out.width="85%", fig.cap="**Figure 3.** Posterior probability of each change year from the combined MCMC draws (grey bars) and from exact numerical integration on a grid (orange points)."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "bayes_mcmc_vs_grid.png"))
```

## 5. Posterior Results and Interpretation

```{r loo-table}
loo_w |>
  transmute(Model = model,
            `elpd (LOO)` = sprintf("%.1f", elpd_loo),
            `Difference from best (SE)` = ifelse(elpd_diff == 0, "0",
                                                 sprintf("%.1f (%.1f)", elpd_diff, se_diff)),
            `p_loo` = sprintf("%.1f", p_loo),
            `Stacking weight` = sprintf("%.2f", stacking)) |>
  kable(caption = "**Table 2.** Leave-one-out cross-validation (PSIS-LOO). Higher expected log predictive density (elpd) is better; stacking weights combine the models for prediction.")
```

**Did temperature change?** Yes. The no-change model B0 is worst by
`r f1(-loo_w$elpd_diff[loo_w$model == "B0"])` elpd units (Table 2)
[@vehtari2017loo]. Under the linear trend B1, the warming rate is
`r pci("B1", "trend_decade", f = f2)` °C per decade, with $P(\beta > 0 \mid y)$
`r ifelse(pp(1) > 0.999, "> 0.999", f2(pp(1)))`. Every model agrees on how
much warming has accumulated. The posterior mean difference between 2026 and
1938 is `r pci("B1", "total_warming")` °C under B1,
`r pci("B3", "total_warming")` °C under B3 and
`r pci("B4", "total_warming")` °C under B4.

**Gradual or abrupt?** The data cannot tell. Models with curvature or a
change point (B2–B5) beat the straight line B1 by about
`r f1(loo_w$elpd_loo[loo_w$model == "B4"] - loo_w$elpd_loo[loo_w$model == "B1"])`
elpd. Among themselves, though, they lie within about one standard error of
each other. Stacking [@yao2018stacking] puts most weight on the gradual
slope-change model B4 (`r f2(loo_w$stacking[loo_w$model == "B4"])`) and the
rest on the jump model B3 (`r f2(loo_w$stacking[loo_w$model == "B3"])`).

**When, and how large?** The jump model B3 has two explanations of almost
equal posterior probability (Figures 4–6):

* With probability `r f2(w_b3[["late"]])`, a **jump of
  `r pci("B3", "jump", "late", f2)` °C** after
  `r round(ps("B3", "cp_year", "late")$median)` on top of an essentially flat
  trend (`r pci("B3", "trend_decade", "late", f2)` °C/decade).
* With probability `r f2(w_b3[["early"]])`, a **drop of
  `r f2(-ps("B3", "jump", "early")$mean)` °C** in the mid-1960s, after the
  hot drought summers of the 1950s, followed by steady warming of
  `r pci("B3", "trend_decade", "early", f2)` °C/decade.

The gradual model B4 places the start of faster warming around
`r round(ps("B4", "cp_year")$median)` (95% CrI
`r ci(ps("B4", "cp_year")$lower, ps("B4", "cp_year")$upper, function(x) sprintf("%.0f", x))`).
The rate increases by `r pci("B4", "slope_change_decade", f = f2)` °C/decade
($P > 0 =$ `r f2(pp(8))`).

**Prediction.** The posterior predictive distribution for summer 2027 has
mean `r f1(bayes$pred_2027$mean[bayes$pred_2027$model == "B3"])` °C under B3
(95% interval
`r ci(bayes$pred_2027$lower[bayes$pred_2027$model == "B3"], bayes$pred_2027$upper[bayes$pred_2027$model == "B3"])`).
The probability that 2027 exceeds 36 °C is
`r f2(bayes$pred_2027$p_above_36[bayes$pred_2027$model == "B3"])`, compared
with `r f2(bayes$pred_2027$p_above_36[bayes$pred_2027$model == "B1"])` under B1.

**Answer.** Austin summers are about 2 °C hotter than in 1938, and this
conclusion is robust. Whether the change came as one abrupt jump in 2007 or
as gradual warming that accelerated after the 1970s is genuinely uncertain
given 89 noisy summers. The timing of any single change point should not be
over-interpreted.

```{r fig-fits, out.width="90%", fig.cap="**Figure 4.** Posterior mean (lines) and 95% credible bands for the mean summer TMAX under the linear trend B1, the slope-change model B4, and the two modes of the jump model B3 (with their posterior probabilities)."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "bayes_fits.png"))
```

```{r fig-changeyear, out.width="85%", fig.cap="**Figure 5.** Distribution of the change year: conventional parametric bootstrap of $\\hat\\gamma$ for M3 (top) and Bayesian posteriors for B3 (middle) and B4 (bottom)."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "bayes_changeyear.png"))
```

```{r fig-prior-post, out.width="95%", fig.cap="**Figure 6.** Prior (grey) and posterior (orange) distributions for the jump model B3. The data move the change point, jump size and total warming far from their priors; the jump posterior is bimodal (a drop in the 1960s or a rise in 2007)."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "bayes_prior_posterior.png"))
```

## 6. Sensitivity Analysis and Model Checking

```{r sens-table}
sens$sensitivity |>
  transmute(Variant = variant,
            `P(change after 1987)` = f2(p_late),
            `Jump if late (°C)` = paste(f2(jump_late), ci(jump_late_lower, jump_late_upper, f2)),
            `Jump if early (°C)` = f2(jump_early),
            `Total warming (°C)` = paste(f2(total_warming), ci(tw_lower, tw_upper, f2)),
            `AR(1) ρ` = ifelse(is.na(rho), "–", paste(f2(rho), ci(rho_lower, rho_upper, f2)))) |>
  kable(caption = "**Table 3.** Sensitivity of the jump model B3. Each row changes one assumption relative to the main analysis. Intervals are 95% credible intervals.")
```

**Priors and assumptions.** We refit B3 four more times (Table 3): with
the change point allowed anywhere in 1939–2025, with all coefficient prior
SDs four times smaller, with them four times larger, and with AR(1) errors
($\rho \sim \text{Uniform}(-1, 1)$).

```{r sens-values}
sv <- sens$sensitivity
tight <- sv[sv$variant == "Priors 4x tighter", ]
```

Total warming stays at about 2 °C in every variant
(`r f1(min(sv$total_warming))`–`r f1(max(sv$total_warming))` °C). The jump
in the late mode is consistently
`r f1(min(sv$jump_late))`–`r f1(max(sv$jump_late))` °C. The change-point
window and AR(1) errors change essentially nothing. With a change point in
the model, $\rho =$ `r with(sv[sv$variant == "AR(1) errors", ], paste(f2(rho), ci(rho_lower, rho_upper, f2)))`,
which supports independent errors.

**The relative weight of the two modes is *not* robust.** Under the 4×
tighter priors, P(change after 1987) rises from `r f2(sv$p_late[1])` to
`r f2(tight$p_late)`. Those priors restrict slopes to about ±0.25 °C per
decade, which rules out the steep post-1960s warming (about 0.5 °C/decade)
that the early mode needs. The 4× wider priors move it the other way, to
`r f2(sv$p_late[sv$variant == "Priors 4x wider"])`. The data alone cannot
decide between "a jump in 2007" and "a 1960s drop followed by fast warming".
The choice hinges on how plausible a sustained 0.5 °C/decade warming rate
is.

For the linear model B1, AR(1) errors give
$\rho =$ `r with(filter(sens$b1_ar_summary, quantity == "rho"), paste(f2(mean), ci(lower, upper, f2)))`
and leave the warming rate essentially unchanged
(`r with(filter(sens$b1_ar_summary, quantity == "trend_decade", errors == "AR(1)"), paste(f2(mean), ci(lower, upper, f2)))`
°C/decade).

**Posterior predictive checks.** For 4,000 replicated series from each
model [@gabry2019visualization] we computed four statistics (Figure 7): the
SD, the hottest summer, the lag-1 autocorrelation, and the 2008–2026 mean
minus the earlier mean.
B3 and B4 reproduce all four, with posterior predictive p-values between
`r f2(min(ppl$p_value[ppl$model != "B1"]))` and
`r f2(max(ppl$p_value[ppl$model != "B1"]))`. The linear model B1 reproduces
the spread, the hottest summer and the persistence between summers (lag-1
$p =$ `r f2(ppl$p_value[ppl$model == "B1" & grepl("Lag-1", ppl$stat)])`).
It rarely produces a recent period as warm as the observed 2008–2026
($p =$ `r f2(ppl$p_value[ppl$model == "B1" & grepl("Mean 2008", ppl$stat)])`).
A straight line underestimates recent summers, which agrees with LOO. This
statistic was chosen after seeing the data, so the result is descriptive.

```{r fig-ppc, out.width="100%", fig.cap="**Figure 7.** Posterior predictive checks: distribution of each test statistic over 4,000 replicated data sets (grey) and the observed value (orange line)."}
include_graphics(file.path(fig_dir, "bayes_ppc_stats.png"))
```

## 7. Alternative Analysis, Comparison, and Bayesian Justification

**Conventional analysis.** We fitted the same six mean models (M0–M5) by
maximum likelihood with generalized least squares [@pinheiro2000nlme], with
iid or AR(1) errors. For change-point models the likelihood was profiled over
candidate years, and models were compared with AICc. A change was tested with
the Andrews sup-F test [@andrews1993tests; @zeileis2002strucchange] and a
parametric bootstrap of the sup-likelihood-ratio statistic, needed because
$\gamma$ does not exist under the null. The uncertainty in $\hat\gamma$ also
came from a parametric bootstrap (B = `r conv$B`). Mann–Kendall with Sen's
slope [@mann1945trend; @sen1968slope] gave a nonparametric cross-check.

AICc selects M3 (jump, iid errors) with $\hat\gamma =$
`r conv$best_cp$gamma`, i.e. a jump after the summer of
`r conv$best_cp$gamma`. Its nearest competitors are M4 and M2, at
`r f1(conv$comparison$dAICc[conv$comparison$model == "M4" & conv$comparison$errors == "iid"])`
and
`r f1(conv$comparison$dAICc[conv$comparison$model == "M2" & conv$comparison$errors == "iid"])`
AICc units. "No change" is strongly rejected (sup-F
$p =$ `r sprintf("%.4f", conv$supF$p.value)`; bootstrap
$p <$ `r sprintf("%.3f", 1 / conv$B)`; Mann–Kendall
$p =$ `r sprintf("%.4f", conv$nonparam$mk_p[1])`).

```{r comparison-table}
pred_conv <- {
  m1 <- lm(y ~ s, data = annual)
  m3 <- lm(y ~ s + I(year > conv$best_cp$gamma), data = annual)
  new <- data.frame(s = 2027 - st$mid_year, year = 2027)
  list(M1 = predict(m1, new, interval = "prediction"),
       M3 = predict(m3, new, interval = "prediction"))
}
b <- bayes$pred_2027
comp <- tribble(
  ~Quantity, ~Conventional, ~Bayesian,
  "Warming rate, linear trend (°C/decade)",
    paste(f2(conv_m1$estimate), ci(conv_m1$lower, conv_m1$upper, f2), "[M1, AR(1)]"),
    paste(pci("B1", "trend_decade", f = f2), "[B1]"),
  "Change year γ (jump model)",
    paste0(conv$best_cp$gamma, " (bootstrap ", conv$gamma_ci[1], ", ", conv$gamma_ci[3], ")"),
    paste0("P(2000–2012) = ", f2(pp(5)), "; P(1952–1975) = ", f2(pp(6))),
  "Jump size (°C)",
    paste(f2(conv_m3$estimate[conv_m3$term == "step"]),
          ci(conv_m3$lower[conv_m3$term == "step"], conv_m3$upper[conv_m3$term == "step"], f2),
          "given γ = 2007"),
    paste(pci("B3", "jump", "late", f2), "if late;", f2(ps("B3", "jump", "early")$mean), "if early"),
  "Total warming 1938–2026 (°C)",
    paste(f2(88 * conv_m1$estimate / 10), ci(88 * conv_m1$lower / 10, 88 * conv_m1$upper / 10, f2), "[M1]"),
    paste(pci("B3", "total_warming", f = f2), "[B3]"),
  "Preferred description",
    paste0("M3 jump (AICc); M4 at +", f1(conv$comparison$dAICc[conv$comparison$model == "M4" & conv$comparison$errors == "iid"])),
    "B2–B5 tied (LOO); stacking favours B4",
  "Prediction for 2027 (°C)",
    paste(f1(pred_conv$M3[1]), ci(pred_conv$M3[2], pred_conv$M3[3]), "[M3, γ fixed]"),
    paste(f1(b$mean[b$model == "B3"]), ci(b$lower[b$model == "B3"], b$upper[b$model == "B3"]), "[B3]")
)
kable(comp, caption = "**Table 4.** Conventional versus Bayesian results. Intervals are 95% confidence/credible/prediction intervals.")
```

**Comparison.** The analyses agree on the main facts (Table 4). The warming
rates are almost identical, both reject "no change", and conditional on a
2007 change both find a jump of about 2 °C. The differences concern the
change point:

1. **Timing uncertainty.** Most of the bootstrap distribution of
   $\hat\gamma$ sits on 2007 (Figure 5), but the posterior gives the
   mid-1960s almost equal probability. The profile likelihood supports the
   posterior: 1964 is only
   `r f1(-max(conv$profiles$loglik[conv$profiles$model == "M3" & conv$profiles$errors == "iid" & conv$profiles$gamma == 1964] - max(conv$profiles$loglik[conv$profiles$model == "M3" & conv$profiles$errors == "iid"])))`
   log-likelihood units below 2007. Resampling around the single best fit
   understates this second mode.
2. **Conditioning on $\hat\gamma$.** The conventional jump and prediction
   intervals treat $\gamma = 2007$ as known. The Bayesian ones average over
   $c$, so the jump is either about +2 °C or about −1.8 °C.
3. **Model choice.** AICc rewards the sharp fit at 2007. LOO averages over
   $c$ and finds an effective complexity of
   $p_\text{loo} \approx$ `r f1(loo_w$p_loo[loo_w$model == "B3"])` for B3, far
   above its 5 nominal parameters, so it does not prefer the jump. (In B3 and
   B5 a few Pareto $\hat k$ values exceed 0.7, max
   `r f2(max(loo_w$max_pareto_k))`, so those elpd values are less reliable.)

**Why is the Bayesian approach justified here?** The scientific question is
about the *uncertainty* in a change's timing and size. $\gamma$ is a
discrete, non-regular parameter, so asymptotic intervals do not apply, and
the bootstrap misses the second mode. The posterior gives direct
probabilities, for example P(total warming > 1 °C) = `r f2(pp(4))`, and its
predictions carry the timing uncertainty with them. It also exposes that
the mode weights depend on the slope prior (Table 3). The advantage is
limited, however. For the headline conclusion, about 2 °C of clearly
non-zero warming, both approaches agree, and the conventional analysis is
simpler. The Bayesian analysis mainly guards against overconfidence about
*when* the change happened.
